summary: Defines an XML format for civic location (street addresses) for use in PIDF-LO documents, replacing the format in RFC 4119. It adds elements based on civic types defined for DHCP. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC rewrites the XML format used to write a postal address inside a presence document. It adds the missing parts of an address, such as the building, the room and the seat, and it lets a street name be broken into sections and branches so that the same number on the same street can still be found.

questions: how to represent civic addresses in xml
what changed in rfc 5139 civic location
how to write a civic address in xml
subtitle: A richer XML format for street addresses inside a presence location object.

tldr.problem: The original format for civic locations in presence documents left out several parts of a postal address, and it had no way to describe a street whose sections, branches and sub-branches repeat the same house numbers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC revises the civic form of the PIDF-LO document with the extra elements collected in RFC 4776, a hierarchy of thoroughfare elements, and a schema whose values are whitespace-normalised.
tldr.outcome: A presence document can now carry a street address precise enough to name a building, a unit or a seat, and to disambiguate a road that repeats its numbers across sections.

today: RFC 5139 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4119 with the civic address elements described here. It has not itself been obsoleted or updated, so the format it defines is the one this document describes.

sections.title: What Is Being Revised
sections.content:
Since the publication of the original PIDF-LO civic specification in RFC 4119, it has been found that the specification lacks a number of additional parameters that can be used to specify a civic location more precisely. Those additional parameters have largely been captured in RFC 4776, the DHCP option for civic address configuration.

This document revises the GEOPRIV civic form to include the additional civic parameters of RFC 4776. It also introduces a hierarchical structure for identifying a road, a structure that is used in some countries, and defines new elements that allow still more precision in a civic location.

The document uses the term thoroughfare to mean a road, or part of a road, or another access route along which the final point is identified, which is the same sense used by the Universal Postal Union.
sections.plainLanguage: When the first version of this format was written, it turned out to be missing several parts of a real address. This RFC adds them back in, and adds a way to describe a street that has several sections with the same numbers on each.

sections.title: The New Civic Address Types
sections.content:
RFC 4776 lists several civic address types that need support in the formal PIDF-LO definition and that are not in RFC 4119. The document adds them as new elements, each with a code in the civic address type registry.

Four of the new elements describe the destination inside a building: BLD for the building or structure, with the example Hope Theatre; UNIT for the unit, apartment or suite, for example 12a; ROOM for the room, for example 450F; and SEAT for the seat, desk or workstation, for example WS 181. Two more name the kind of place and the community: PLC for the place type, for example office, and PCN for the postal community name, for example Leonia. Two handle the post: POBOX for a post office box, for example U40, and ADDCODE for an additional code, for example 13203000003.

The remaining six are about the road itself and are described in the next section: RD for the primary road or street, RDSEC for a road section, RDBR for a road branch, RDSUBBR for a road sub-branch, PRM for a road pre-modifier and POM for a road post-modifier. Their codes run from 25 to 39, and the table in Section 3.1 lists each element with its code, its meaning and an example. A complete description of the types is in RFC 4776.
sections.plainLanguage: The new elements fill in the parts of an address that were missing: which building, which unit, which room, which seat, what kind of place it is, the post office box, and the parts of the road name that come before and after the main street name.

sections.title: Breaking a Road Name into Parts
sections.content:
In some countries a thoroughfare is broken into sections, and street numbers are repeated between the sections. A road section identifier is needed so that an address is unique. The example given is a street with five sections, each numbered from one, so that without the section the number seven could exist in five different places. The RDSEC element names that section.

Minor streets can share a name, so that they can only be told apart by the major thoroughfare they intersect. Both a street section and another street could be crossed by the same lane, so the RDBR element names a road branch where the branch name does not uniquely identify the road. Road branches may also be used where a major thoroughfare is split into sections. A road sub-branch is associated with a road branch in the same way, and the RDSUBBR element identifies it.

Two rules follow from this. The street numbering, held in the HNO element, applies to the most specific road element given, that is, the first one of RDSUBBR, RDBR, RDSEC or RD that is specified. And the PRM, POM, PRD, POD and STS elements always apply to the value of the RD element alone. If a road branch or sub-branch needs a suffix or a qualifier, that text must be included in the RDBR or RDSUBBR element instead.

The A6 element is retained for the countries that require that level of detail, but where A6 was previously used for street names in RFC 4119 it must not be used; the RD element must be used for thoroughfare data.
sections.plainLanguage: Some streets are split into sections that each start their numbering again, and side streets can share a name. So the format has an element for the section, one for a branch off the main road and one for a lane off that branch. The house number belongs to the most specific of those that is given.

sections.title: The Country and the Top-Level Subdivision
sections.content:
The country element differs from the one defined in RFC 4119: it now restricts the value to two uppercase characters, which are the alpha-2 codes of ISO 3166-1.

The A1 element holds the top-level subdivision within a country. In the absence of a country-specific guide on how to use the A-series of elements, the second part of the ISO 3166-2 code for a country subdivision should be used. That code is made of a country code and a hyphen plus a code of one, two or three characters or numerals. For the A1 element the leading country code and the hyphen are omitted, and only the subdivision code is included.

The examples given show how different countries code their subdivisions. Canada uses CA-BC, CA-ON and CA-QC. Luxembourg has just three single-character codes, LU-D, LU-G and LU-L. Australia uses both two-character and three-character codes, AU-ACT, AU-NSW and AU-NT. France uses numerical codes for mainland France and letters for its territories, FR-75 and FR-NC. These produce the fragments <country>CA</country><A1>ON</A1>, <country>LU</country><A1>L</A1>, <country>AU</country><A1>ACT</A1> and <country>FR</country><A1>75</A1>.
sections.plainLanguage: The country is written as the two-letter code from the ISO list, such as AU. The region within the country uses the ISO subdivision code with the country part left off, so New South Wales is NSW and Paris is 75.

sections.title: Languages, Scripts and Whitespace
sections.content:
The schema allows the xml:lang attribute on every element except country and PLC, which hold language-neutral values. The script field of RFC 4776 is omitted in favour of using the xml:lang attribute with a script subtag, as described in RFC 4646.

It is recommended that each civicAddress element uses one language only, or a combination of languages that is consistent. Where a civic location is represented in several languages, several civicAddress elements should be included in the PIDF-LO document, and for civic addresses that together describe the same location they should go into the same tuple.

The DHCP format allows an element to appear several times with different languages or scripts, while the XML form permits only one instance of each element, so a conversion needs several civicAddress elements if any element is duplicated in a different language. One civicAddress element is created for each language present, holding all the elements in that language, and the language-independent elements such as country and PLC are added to all of them. Where the receiver is known and has stated its language preferences, for instance through the Accept-Language header of SIP or HTTP, a single document can be built from those preferences: every value that occurs once is used, and where several values exist each is weighted by the preferences and the highest one is chosen. An arbitrary value is selected if two values have the same preference, if there is no preference for the available languages, or if there are conflicting values in the same language.

The schema uses the base type token rather than string, which RFC 4119 used. The token type makes sure that whitespace inside a document is normalized and collapsed before it reaches a processor, so that three fragments that differ only in spacing are treated as the same value. Whitespace can still be included in a value by writing a character reference such as  .
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of the address can say which language it is written in, and an address given in two languages is written as two civicAddress elements. The format also tidies up whitespace, so that an address written with extra spaces is treated the same as one written tightly.

sections.title: The Schema and Its Registration
sections.content:
The schema for civic addresses has the target namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:geopriv10:civicAddr. The civicAddress element holds a sequence of optional elements in a fixed order: country, then A1 to A6, then the qualifiers and the road, then the house number and its suffix, then the landmark and location, the floor and the name, the postal code, then the building, unit, room and seat, the place type, the postal community name, the post office box and the additional code. Elements from other namespaces may follow, and any attributes from any namespace are allowed.

The country element uses a simple type restricted to two uppercase letters, while the other elements use a type based on token with an optional xml:lang attribute, except PLC which uses token alone.

The document registers the namespace with IANA under the guidelines of RFC 3688, with the registrant contact of the IETF GEOPRIV working group, and registers the XML schema under urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:pidf:geopriv10:civicAddr, with the schema itself being the whole of Section 4. It also updates the civic address type registry established by RFC 4776, adding the new types to the PIDF column of the registry table.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives the XML schema that says which elements may appear, in which order, and what each one may hold. It also registers the namespace and the schema with IANA, and adds the new address types to the registry.

sections.title: A Worked Address
sections.content: The example in Section 5 is a civic address in English for Australia, with the country AU and the state NSW. It names the locality Wollongong and the district North Wollongong, the thoroughfare Flinders Street, a branch called Campbell Street, the landmark Gilligan's Island, the location Corner, the name of the place Video Rental Store, the postal code 2500, the room Westerns and Classics, the place type store, and a post office box, Private Box 15. The whitespace inside some elements is deliberate in the example, and the token type collapses it when the document is processed.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows an address for a video rental store: the country and state, the town and district, the street and the lane off it, a landmark, the name of the shop, the postal code, the room, and a post office box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The XML representation described in this document is designed for inclusion in a PIDF-LO document, and it is therefore subject to the same security considerations as those described in RFC 4119. Considerations about including the representation in other XML documents are outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: These addresses say where somebody is, so the format inherits the same privacy and security rules as the presence location format it was written for. Using it in other kinds of XML document is not covered here.

items.title: A1
items.text: The ISO 3166-2 subdivision code without the country part, such as NSW.

items.title: HNO
items.text: The street number, which applies to the most specific road element given.

items.title: LMK
items.text: A landmark near the address, such as a shop or a building.

items.title: PC
items.text: The postal code of the address.

items.title: PLC
items.text: The kind of place, such as store or office.

viz.caption: THE EXAMPLE CIVIC ADDRESS FROM RFC 5139 SECTION 5

data.title: A civic address
data.code:
<civicAddress xml:lang="en-AU"
  xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:geopriv10:civicAddr">
  <country>AU</country>
  <A1>NSW</A1>
  <A3>Wollongong</A3>
  <A4>North Wollongong</A4>
  <RD>Flinders</RD><STS>Street</STS>
  <RDBR>Campbell Street</RDBR>
  <LMK>Gilligan's Island</LMK>
  <LOC>Corner</LOC>
  <NAM>Video Rental Store</NAM>
  <PC>2500</PC>
  <ROOM>Westerns and Classics</ROOM>
  <PLC>store</PLC>
  <POBOX>Private Box 15</POBOX>
</civicAddress>
